working-holiday-visas.name: The working holiday visa pause
working-holiday-visas.description: Bevan's record on the pause to Work and Holiday visas and the slowdown in Working Holiday processing: the backpacker workforce that picks, packs and pours across the South West and Great Southern, and what a stalled application queue does to a harvest that cannot wait.
working-holiday-visas.intro:
Australia runs two working holiday visas. The Working Holiday visa, subclass 417, covers countries such as the United Kingdom, Ireland and Canada, and is not capped. The Work and Holiday visa, subclass 462, covers a separate list of partner countries and is capped country by country, from 100 places a year to 5,000.

In the 2026-27 program year, which opened on 1 July 2026, the Department of Home Affairs moved 24 of the 29 subclass 462 partner countries to a paused status, so applications from those countries are not being taken. Processing of subclass 417 applications slowed at the same time. There was no announcement. The change appeared on the Home Affairs website and was picked up by ABC News in mid August.

## What the Government has said

Home Affairs says the reforms will "better control demand and provide a fairer allocation of WHM visas" while supporting "critical workforce needs, including in agriculture". The Minister for Home Affairs, Tony Burke, confirmed the visas are being processed more slowly than before and has not said more. No end date has been given. The caps apply to first year visas, so people already in Australia on a second or third year visa are not affected.

## What it means for the regions

The National Farmers' Federation puts backpackers at about half the casual workforce at peak harvest. Across agriculture they are 14 per cent of the farm workforce, rising to 44 per cent in horticulture, 31 per cent in grains, 26 per cent in red meat and 25 per cent in cotton at peak. There were 206,187 working holiday makers in Australia at 30 June 2025. In 2019 the program contributed $3.2 billion to the economy, of which $726 million was spent in regional areas.

## Why the timing matters here

Seasonal work does not wait. Growers apply for workers in July and August so they arrive in time for the season. The WA Grains Group has warned that if approvals do not come through until November or December, it is too late to be of any use to the grains industry. Horticulture, hospitality, and the hostels that house the workforce across the South West and Great Southern all move on the same clock.

## The consultation question

The National Farmers' Federation, the Australian Meat Industry Council and Australian Dairy Farmers have all said they were not consulted before the change. That is the heart of Bevan's objection. Not that immigration settings can never move, but that agriculture was not at the table, and the regions carry the cost of a decision made without them.
